# `PIXterm` - *draw images in your ANSI terminal with true color*

**`PIXterm`** ***shows images directly in your terminal***, recreating the pixels through a combination of [ANSI character background color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Colors) and the [unicode lower half block element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_Elements). If image has transparency, an optional matte color can be used for background. Also, you can specify a dithering mode; in which case, the image is rendered using block elements with different shades, or using standard ASCII characters in the same way. In dithering mode, the matte color is used to fill the background of the blocks or characters.

Supported image formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, WebP.

Fetching images from HTTP/HTTPS is supported too.

## Usage

```
pixterm [options] <image file or URL>
```

### Options

- `-version` - show PIXterm version
- `-credits` - show some love to contributors <3
- `-d <mode>` - dithering mode:
  - `0` - no dithering (default)
  - `1` - with blocks
  - `2` - with chars
- `-go` - output Go code to 'fmt.Print()' the image
- `-m <color>` - matte color for transparency or background (optional, hex format, default: 000000)
- `-nobg` - disable background color (optional, only in dithering mode, ignores matte color)
- `-s <method>` - scale method:
  - `0` - resize (default)
  - `1` - fill
  - `2` - fit
- `-tr <rows>` - terminal rows (optional, >=2; when piping, default: 24)
- `-tc <columns>` - terminal columns (optional, >=2; when piping, default: 80)

## Requirements

Your terminal emulator must support *true color* in order to display image colors correctly. In addition, you must use a monospaced font that includes the lower half block unicode character: `▄ (U+2584)`. [Envy Code R](https://damieng.com/blog/2008/05/26/envy-code-r-preview-7-coding-font-released) is recommended. If you want to use the dithering mode with blocks, the font must also include the following unicode characters: `█ (U+2588)`, `▓ (U+2593)`, `▒ (U+2592)`, `░ (U+2591)`. // dumpComposite prints scaled image composited over matte using given method
func dumpComposite(dst *image.NRGBA, w, h int, mr, mg, mb float64, method string) {
	for y := 0; y < h; y++ {
		for x := 0; x < w; x++ {
			c := dst.NRGBAAt(x, y)
			if x > 0 {
				fmt.Print(" ")
			}
			a := float64(c.A)
			var r, g, b float64
			switch method {
			case "trunc":
				r = math.Floor((float64(c.R)*a + mr*(255-a)) / 255)
				g = math.Floor((float64(c.G)*a + mg*(255-a)) / 255)
				b = math.Floor((float64(c.B)*a + mb*(255-a)) / 255)
			case "round":
				r = math.Floor((float64(c.R)*a+mr*(255-a))/255 + 0.5)
				g = math.Floor((float64(c.G)*a+mg*(255-a))/255 + 0.5)
				b = math.Floor((float64(c.B)*a+mb*(255-a))/255 + 0.5)
			case "rgba16":
				// using color.RGBA() 16-bit premultiplied then >>8 ... like Go's color model conversions
				rr, gg, bb, aa := c.RGBA()
				// composite: dst = src + matte*(0xffff-aa)/0xffff  in 16-bit
				r = float64((uint32(rr) + uint32(mr)*0x101*(0xffff-aa)/0xffff) >> 8)

			case "alphaonly":
				r, g, b = float64(c.R), float64(c.G), a
			}
			fmt.Printf("%d,%d,%d", int(r), int(g), int(b))
		}
		fmt.Println()
	}
}
